How does Vermont property tax work?

Vermont property tax has two layers on one bill: a statewide education tax and a municipal tax set by each town. The town listers set the appraised value on the grand list, and the town collects both parts.

The Department of Taxes, through its Property Valuation and Review division, oversees the system. Its 2025 annual report, based on 2024 grand list data, counts 328,613 properties with a total municipal listed value of about $101.97 billion. Gross taxes that year were $1.662 billion for education and $685 million for municipal purposes, for a combined $2.347 billion before credits.

Because Vermont has 247 municipalities, including 237 towns and 10 cities, the bill you receive depends heavily on the town where the house sits. The state sets the education rate framework. Your selectboard and voters set the municipal side.

What do the statewide numbers look like?

Measure (2024 grand list)Figure
Properties on the grand list328,613
Total municipal listed valueAbout $101.97 billion
Statewide common level of appraisal72.36 percent
Nonhomestead education tax rate1.391 percent
Homestead education base rate1.00 percent
Effective total rate, homestead1.66 percent
Effective total rate, nonhomestead1.70 percent
Education property tax credits$166.9 million

The common level of appraisal compares listed value with fair market value. At 72.36 percent, a typical house sells for more than its listed value, and the state uses that ratio to adjust education rates. It does not change the value on your bill.

What is the homestead declaration and why does it matter at sale time?

A homestead declaration tells the state that you own and live in the house as your domicile, and it lets you pay the homestead education rate instead of the nonhomestead rate. Every Vermont property is treated as nonhomestead unless the owner declares it a homestead.

For 2026 the declaration was due April 15, with October 15 as the last accepted date. A town can charge a late penalty of up to 3 percent if the nonhomestead rate is higher than the homestead rate, or up to 8 percent if it is lower. After the October deadline the property is classified as nonhomestead and the owner pays the higher rate plus any penalty and interest.

  • The owner generally must be a Vermont resident who owns and occupies the home as a domicile on April 1.
  • A home leased more than 182 days in the calendar year, used exclusively for commercial or rental purposes, or used as a second home or camp is nonhomestead.
  • If you sold the home before April 1, you generally cannot keep a homestead declaration for it.

The same Form HS-122 carries the property tax credit claim. The Department's 2025 report says about two-thirds of homesteads receive a credit and that households with income under $47,000 may get an additional credit and a municipal credit.

How do I appeal a Vermont property assessment?

You appeal in steps, starting with the town listers and moving to the board of civil authority and then to the state or the Superior Court. Each step has a short deadline.

  1. Listers hear people who are aggrieved by their appraisals on or before May 20, and such hearings are not held later than June 2 (32 V.S.A. § 4221).
  2. After the listers' final decision, you may appeal in writing to the board of civil authority within 14 days after the date of notice, by lodging the appeal with the town clerk (32 V.S.A. § 4404).
  3. From the board's decision, an appeal to the Director of Property Valuation and Review or the Superior Court begins by notice within 30 days (32 V.S.A. § 4461).

The Vermont League of Cities and Towns describes the board of civil authority as a body that must hold a hearing and inspect each appealed parcel, and that may sustain, increase or decrease the listers' value. Few cases reach the state level: the Department's report counts 36 appeals on the 2023 grand list and 19 on the 2024 grand list as of January 8, 2025.

Are Vermont towns reappraising, and will a new value change my bill?

Many towns are overdue, and the state is pushing them toward regular reappraisals. The report says Act 68 requires full reappraisals every six years starting January 1, 2025, unless the Division approves a longer period.

The Department says the average last reappraisal year across the state is 2016, and 60 towns last reappraised more than 15 years ago. The state planned to send 152 reappraisal orders in summer 2025, and towns were booking reappraisals for 2026 through 2029.

For a seller, a reappraisal can move the listed value closer to market value. Check the date of your town's last reappraisal on the town website or ask the listers before you assume your tax bill matches what the buyer will pay.

What happens to the education tax rates next year?

The state projects that the average education property tax bill will rise by 11.9 percent in fiscal year 2027. Commissioner of Taxes Bill Shouldice released that projection in the December 1, 2025 education tax rate letter and wrote that education taxes would have gone up nearly 41 percent over five years if the increase takes effect.

The percentage is a statewide average, so individual bills vary. The Department says homestead rates depend on local education spending and the nonhomestead rate is uniform statewide. Buyers who look at the bill on a listing sheet may be looking at last year's number, so a seller does well to show the current bill from the town clerk or treasurer.

What does Vermont's Current Use program mean for a seller?

Current Use, formally the Use Value Appraisal program, taxes enrolled farm and forest land on its productive use value instead of market value. The program started in 1978, and the 2025 report counts 19,692 enrolled parcels covering 2,574,742 acres, about one-third of Vermont's land.

  • Enrolled land stays in the program after a sale unless the owner or the Division withdraws it.
  • The new owner must submit a transfer application and required documents within 30 days after the transfer is recorded.
  • Once an application is approved and recorded, a contingent lien is placed on the land.
  • If the new owner develops the land or changes its use, the land use change tax may apply. The report puts that tax at 10 percent of the fair market value of developed land.

The 2024 use values were $188 an acre for forest land, $141 an acre for forest more than one mile from a road, and $483 an acre for agricultural land. A house on a larger wooded lot may be partly enrolled, so ask your listers whether any of your acreage is in the program before you list.

What taxes are due at closing on a Vermont sale?

The main tax at closing is the property transfer tax, which is due within 30 days of the closing date. For a buyer's principal residence the rate is 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 and 1.25 percent above that, plus a 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge on the amount above $200,000. A year-round home that is not the buyer's principal residence and not a long-term rental is taxed at 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.

If the seller is a nonresident, the buyer withholds 2.5 percent of the sale price and files Form RW-171 within 30 days, unless the seller has a Commissioner's Certificate. The Department's report counts $62.4 million in property transfer tax and $31.1 million in real estate withholding for fiscal year 2024, which shows how routine both are.

Recording a deed costs $15.00 per page and a transfer tax return costs a flat $15.00, according to a 2025 town fee schedule, and your town clerk can confirm the figures.

What if I owe back property tax and want to sell?

You can sell a Vermont house with tax due, and the unpaid amount can be settled from the proceeds at closing.

  • A collector may charge a commission of up to 8 percent of the tax after the deadline in the collector's notice, and voters may set a lower rate or a grace period (32 V.S.A. § 1674).
  • The collector mails a notice at least 30 days before the payment date, and if no date is set payment is due 30 days after mailing (32 V.S.A. § 4772).
  • A tax sale needs a delinquency of at least $1,500 for more than one year, and the collector must first offer a written repayment plan (32 V.S.A. § 5252).
  • The sale is advertised in a local newspaper three weeks in a row, and the delinquent owner and any mortgagee get certified-mail notice at least 30 days before the sale.

After a tax sale the owner, lienholder or mortgagee may redeem within one year by paying the sale price plus interest at 1 percent per month. Landlords selling a rental should also know that owners of rented property file a Landlord Certificate (Form LRC-140) with the Department each year.

More questions about Vermont Property Tax Guide

When is the Vermont homestead declaration due?

For 2026 it was due April 15, and the last accepted date was October 15. After that, the property is classified as nonhomestead and the owner pays the higher rate plus any penalty.

How long do I have to appeal my Vermont assessment to the board of civil authority?

You have 14 days after the date of the listers' notice, and you lodge the appeal in writing with the town clerk under 32 V.S.A. § 4404.

Can I sell a house in Vermont if I owe property taxes?

Yes. The unpaid tax can be settled from the sale proceeds at closing. A tax sale needs at least $1,500 delinquent for more than one year, and owners can redeem within one year.

Does a nonresident seller owe Vermont withholding?

Yes, the buyer withholds 2.5 percent of the sale price on Form RW-171 unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate.

What is the Vermont property transfer tax rate?

The Department of Taxes lists 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 of a principal residence and 1.25 percent above, plus a 0.22 percent surcharge on the excess, with a 3.40 percent rate for many non-principal homes.

Does Vermont charge an estate tax, and who actually owes it?

Vermont charges an estate tax, but only on large estates. Under 32 V.S.A. § 7442a, an estate with a Vermont taxable estate under $5,000,000 owes nothing, and an estate of $5,000,000 or more owes 16 percent of the amount above $5,000,000.

The tax is figured on the whole estate, not on one house. A bank account, a retirement plan, a business interest and a Vermont home all count toward the total. An apportionment fraction then limits the tax to the Vermont share of the estate.

For most families who inherit a house in Vermont, the practical answer is that no Vermont estate tax is due. The Census Bureau reports a median value for owner-occupied homes in Vermont of $316,600 for 2020 to 2024. A single house at that level sits far below the $5 million line. Heirs of larger estates, or heirs who share a house with a big investment portfolio, are the people who need to look closer.

What are the main Vermont and federal estate figures at a glance?

These are the figures the state and federal agencies publish for the current period.

ItemFigureSource
Vermont estate tax threshold$5,000,000Vermont Department of Taxes
Vermont rate above the threshold16 percent32 V.S.A. § 7442a
Vermont filing threshold changeRaised to $5 million, effective June 18, 2026Vermont Department of Taxes
Extension of time to fileSix months, Form EST-195Vermont Department of Taxes
Federal basic exclusion for 2026 deaths$15,000,000IRS
Median owner-occupied home value, Vermont$316,600U.S. Census Bureau

The federal exclusion is higher than the Vermont threshold, so an estate can owe Vermont estate tax while owing no federal estate tax.

When must an estate file a Vermont estate tax return?

An estate must file Form EST-191 when the person who died had an interest in Vermont property and the federal gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts made within two years of death exceeds $5 million, or when a federal Form 706 is required. The Department of Taxes says the Legislature in 2026 raised the filing threshold to $5 million so that it matches the payment threshold.

Property located in Vermont for a resident does not include real or tangible property outside Vermont. For a nonresident, intangible property is also left out. A nonresident who owned a Vermont vacation house therefore counts the house, but not the brokerage account held in another state.

An executor also deals with other returns. The Department also lists an income tax return (IN-111) and a fiduciary return (FIT-161) if the estate earns income. If more time is needed for the estate tax return, Form EST-195 gives six months and must be filed on or before the due date.

Does Vermont have an inheritance tax on what heirs receive?

The tax in Vermont is measured on the estate as a whole before anything is handed to heirs.

What federal rules affect an heir who sells a Vermont house?

The federal estate tax exclusion for people who die in 2026 is $15,000,000, according to the IRS, and a surviving spouse may elect to use the unused portion of the exclusion of the spouse who died.

The federal income tax on the sale is a different matter. The IRS explains in Topic 701 that the home sale exclusion of up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, depends on ownership and use tests of two years within five. An heir who never lived in the house usually does not meet those tests, so the gain on the sale is figured separately.

How does probate work when the estate owns a Vermont house?

When someone dies owning real estate in their own name, Vermont requires a formal estate, and the Probate Division of the Superior Court in the county where the person lived handles it. The Vermont Judiciary says a formal estate applies if the person owned real estate or the estate is worth more than $45,000.

The court recognizes an executor named in a will, or appoints an administrator if there is no will. Surviving spouses and next of kin have priority when suitable, and the personal representative generally posts a bond before appointment.

  • The inventory is due within 30 days of appointment, with assets valued at fair market value on the date of death.
  • The notice to creditors is published in a local newspaper within 30 days of appointment, and creditors then have four months from publication.
  • The personal representative should not pay claims until the four months pass.
  • If publication is skipped and unknown creditors exist, the claim window can stretch to three years after death.

These dates affect a sale because buyers and title companies want to see that debts and claims have been handled before they close.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Vermont houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can the executor sell the house, and what paperwork records the sale?

Yes, but a personal representative who wants to sell, convey, mortgage or lease real estate files a motion for a license with the court. The Judiciary names the Motion for License to Sell or Convey Real Estate (form 700-00035) and a report on the license afterward.

One Vermont title resource describes the next steps this way: after the sale the personal representative signs the deed before an authorized officer and records it with the town or city clerk where the property sits, and the deed refers to the license order. When the debts and expenses are paid, the court issues a decree of distribution, and a certified copy is recorded in the town land records so that title is clear for the heirs.

Vermont land records are kept by town clerks, not by a single county office. Recording a document costs $15.00 per page under 32 V.S.A. § 1671(a)(6), and a property transfer tax return costs a flat $15.00 to record, according to a town fee schedule published in 2025. Your town clerk can confirm the current amounts.

What is the Vermont property transfer tax when an estate sells?

A sale out of an estate to a buyer is a transfer by deed, so the Vermont property transfer tax applies unless an exemption fits. The tax is due within 30 days of the closing date, according to the Department of Taxes.

  • Buyer's principal residence: 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 of value, then 1.25 percent above that, plus a 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge on the amount above $200,000.
  • Year-round home that is not a principal residence and not a long-term rental: 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.
  • Property not fit for year-round habitation: 1.25 percent plus the 0.22 percent surcharge.

The exemption list in 32 V.S.A. § 9603 that we read includes transfers without actual consideration between spouses, parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, and it has no separate line for transfers by will or intestacy.

What if the heir or the estate is not a Vermont resident?

When the seller is a nonresident, the buyer must withhold 2.5 percent of the sale price and send it to the Department of Taxes, unless the seller has a Commissioner's Certificate. The buyer files Form RW-171 with payment within 30 days of the transfer, and the seller claims the amount as a credit on Form IN-111.

A seller can ask for a Commissioner's Certificate through myVTax to reduce or remove withholding. The seller must be in good standing, with all required Vermont returns filed and taxes paid, and must document the property's basis. For an inherited house the Department lists examples such as an estate inventory. Heirs who live out of state should start this step early so the closing is not held up.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What does a seller of an inherited Vermont house also need to disclose or pay?

A seller must give the buyer flood information before or as part of the contract. Under 27 V.S.A. § 380, the seller provides a copy or link to the FEMA flood insurance rate map, says whether the property flooded or suffered flood damage while the seller possessed it, and says whether flood insurance is carried or required. If the seller fails to do this, the buyer can terminate before title or occupancy transfers and can sue for damages and attorney's fees.

Property tax is the other running cost. Vermont education property tax rates differ for homestead and nonhomestead property, and a house that is not declared a homestead is taxed as nonhomestead. A house that no owner lives in as a domicile on April 1 generally falls on the nonhomestead side, so ask the town how an estate-held house is classified.

How does Vermont's size and layout shape an estate sale?

Vermont has 14 counties and 247 municipalities, so an estate sale touches a county probate court and a town clerk that may be in different places. Chittenden County, with Burlington, is the most populous at 168,323 residents in the 2020 Census, and Essex County is the smallest at 5,920.

More questions about Vermont Estate and Inheritance Tax

At what value does Vermont tax an estate?

Vermont taxes an estate only when the Vermont taxable estate reaches $5,000,000. The rate is 16 percent of the amount above $5,000,000, adjusted by an apportionment fraction.

Does an heir pay tax just for inheriting a Vermont house?

No Vermont tax on the act of inheriting appears on the Department of Taxes estate tax page. The estate tax is paid by the estate. Selling the house can still create transfer tax, income tax or withholding questions.

Do I need probate before I sell an inherited house in Vermont?

Usually yes, if the house was in the decedent's own name. The Vermont Judiciary says a formal estate applies when the person owned real estate. The personal representative may need court permission, called a license, to sell.

How long does an executor have to file the inventory?

The inventory is due within 30 days of appointment, per the Vermont Judiciary, with assets valued at fair market value on the date of death.

What is the Vermont withholding rate on a nonresident seller?

The buyer withholds 2.5 percent of the sale price on Form RW-171 unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate. The buyer files within 30 days of the transfer.
